html:
Cassava, also called manioc or yuca, is a shrub grown for its starchy roots. First bred in the south west of the Amazon basin perhaps 8,000 to 10,000 years ago, it is now one of the most important food crops of the tropics.

It grows in poor soil, survives drought, and its roots can stay in the ground until needed. But the bitter kinds contain poison, so people learned to grate, soak, squeeze and cook them into flour and flatbread. It became the staple of lowland South American farmers such as the Tupi, the Taíno and many Amazon peoples, among them the Yudjá and the Puinave.

In the Columbian exchange the Portuguese carried it to Africa in the 1500s, and it spread across Central Africa, where it became a main food. Africa now grows more than half of the world's cassava. It also spread to Asia, where its starch is sold as tapioca, the base of the pearls in bubble tea.
